blocks.text: Isaiah 13 begins a major collection of oracles concerning foreign nations. A common outline places chapters 13-27 after the opening material in chapters 1-12, followed by further large movements in 28-35, 36-39, 40-55, and 56-66. That arrangement is a useful map for reading, but it does not by itself prove either a six-author theory or a single uncontested account of the book's composition.

sections.title: The Opening of the Oracles Against the Nations

blocks.text: The judgment announced against Babylon belongs to Isaiah's wider treatment of Judah, Israel, and the nations. Empires may appear as instruments within divine judgment, yet they remain answerable for their own violence and pride. Elsewhere the book also imagines nations learning, worshiping, and sharing in restoration, so this fierce oracle should not be mistaken for Isaiah's only word about them. The Great Isaiah Scroll and other witnesses attest the book's ancient transmission while also preserving variations; they do not erase the need for careful interpretation of each oracle in its literary setting.
